turns.content:
hey, thanks for taking a look. here's the draft i'm leaving on the bed in the guest room:

'Welcome Brenda! We want you to feel totally at home. Just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. Relax and enjoy!'

honest feedback? is it warm enough or does it read like a list of rules?
I’ll take a look at the note in context of how you’ve been talking about Brenda and the house rules, then give you straight feedback on warmth vs. rule-list energy.

ok maybe i’m being too defensive. but these rules are all from real messes last time. • shoes tracked mud through the whole living room. • she made coffee at 5:30am and woke everyone. • she set the thermostat to 80 and we have pets.

so the note has to cover these. but i hear you that it reads like a dorm contract. • can you pinpoint which line sounds worst?

The worst line is **“no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances.”**

That last bit is what makes it feel like a contract. “Under any circumstances” doesn’t sound like a house preference — it sounds like you’re bracing for an argument. It’s also the only rule with zero *why*, so it lands as a hard ban instead of “hey, last time mud got everywhere.”

Close second: **“please do not touch the smart thermostat.”** “Do not touch” is a little parental, and with no reason it reads like you don’t trust her, not like you’re protecting the pets.

The kitchen line is actually the least harsh of the three, because it at least explains itself. The problem there is the wording (“kitchen stays closed”), not the idea.

If you only soften one phrase, kill **“under any circumstances.”** That’s the dorm-RA energy.

ok you're right about "under any circumstances" being the worst. that and the thermostat line. i softened both:

• "shoes love staying by the door — helps keep the floors clean for everyone"
• "help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am"
• "the thermostat is on a schedule for our pets, so please leave it be"

dropped the "do not touch" entirely. does this actually sound warm now? or still like i'm handing her a handbook?

Warmer line by line, still a handbook as a package.

Each rule is better. You’ve got a *why* now, and you dropped the two phrases that were doing the most damage. If you drop these into the old frame though — *Welcome! Feel at home. Just a reminder: [rule] [rule] [rule]. Relax!* — it still reads as a policy sheet with a smile on it. “Just a reminder” is doing a lot of that.

The leftover handbook energy is mostly:

- **The cute shoe line.** “Shoes love staying by the door” is trying so hard to not be a rule that it *feels* like a rule in a costume. A normal host sentence is warmer than a personified one.
- **“Help us preserve peaceful mornings.”** That’s the new stiffest line. “Preserve” is a little HR / spa-brochure. The 8am idea is fine; the wording is still formal.
- **Three policies in a row.** That’s the real issue now, not any single phrase. One or two nested in a welcome sounds like a house. Three stacked still sounds like orientation.

Thermostat is the one that actually works. Pets + schedule + “leave it be” is clear without sounding like you don’t trust her.

If you want it to *feel* like a welcome note, lead with the guest stuff (towels, wifi, help yourself to X) and tuck one practical ask in naturally — don’t open with “feel at home” and then immediately inventory the restrictions.

• ok. i hear you on the stacking problem. but i have to cover the three things or the week will be chaos again. • if i cut to two rules and lead with guest stuff, which two stay and which one gets dropped?

Drop **shoes** from the bed note. Keep **kitchen after 8** and **the thermostat**.

Not because shoes don’t matter — last time’s mud is real — but because a note on the pillow is the wrong place for that rule. She hits the shoe problem at the door, hours before she reads anything in the guest room. Say it when she walks in (“mudroom’s right here, shoes live there”) or put a tiny cue at the actual threshold. That covers it better than paragraph three of a welcome note.

The two that earn the paper:

- **Kitchen / 8am** — no object to warn her. At 5:30 she’s not rereading your note; she needs the house rhythm said clearly once, in the thing she reads when she arrives. Waking people is also the one that turns the week sour fastest.
- **Thermostat** — not obvious, and it’s pets, not preference. One line with the reason is enough. If you want a backup, that’s the one that also deserves a small note *on the thermostat*, not a third bullet on the bed.

So: guest stuff first, those two tucked in, shoes handled at the door. You still cover all three. You just stop making the welcome note do a job it can’t.

ok i get the logic of moving shoes to the door. that's fine. • but the note has to land on the bed in two hours, and i can't rewrite it ten more times. • can you just tell me if this version sounds warm and ready to leave, or still cold?

Still a little cold. Not ready to leave as-is.

The two remaining lines are fine. What’s missing is an actual welcome. If the paper on the bed is basically “kitchen after 8” and “leave the thermostat,” it still reads like a handbook, just a shorter one.

Don’t touch the rules again. Add two host sentences at the top (glad you’re here, towels/wifi/help yourself to whatever), keep kitchen + thermostat, handle shoes at the door. Then put it down.
